title_prefix: A partially-received message is reaped a
mechanism: Core has no per-message clock. CNode::vRecvMsg / Transport::ReceivedBytes hold a partially received message for as long as the connection lives; the only receive rule is InactivityCheck's now > last_recv + TIMEOUT_INTERVAL (refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:2040-2046 with TIMEOUT_INTERVAL = 20 minutes at refs/bitcoin/src/net.h:58-59), applied uniformly whether or not a message is in progress. Ours adds a rule Core does not have: once any byte of a message has been consumed, connection-receive-in-progress-p is true and connection-receive-expired-p (src/networking/connection.lisp:668-679) reports expiry after +receive-stall-timeout-seconds+ = 300 (:592) measured from connection-recv-last-progress, which drain-and-reap-peer consults after every drain and acts on by disconnecting (src/networking/ibd.lisp:1866-1871). A peer that has not started a message is exempt, which is correct -- that test is what keeps an idle poll from reading as a stall.
consequence: Narrower than the finding suggests, and it matters. connection-recv-last-progress is restamped every time the reader takes ANY byte (src/networking/connection.lisp:806-807), so the rule fires only on 300 seconds of TOTAL silence in the middle of a message, not on slow delivery: the quantification asked for -- a 1 MB block at 3 KB/s, about 350 seconds of transfer -- never trips it, because every arriving segment resets the clock and the gaps are milliseconds. What is dropped is a peer whose link goes completely dead mid-message for between 300 and 1200 seconds and then recovers: Core keeps it, we drop it, and the drop is followed by an immediate redial of the same address. Bounded on both ends -- past 1200 seconds Core drops it too -- so this is a 4x-stricter window on an already-degraded link rather than a rule that costs healthy peers. The finding's complementary claim is REFUTED: it says we have no rule covering Core's last_recv case for a peer that answers pongs, but a pong refreshes Core's last_recv exactly as it refreshes ours, so Core does not drop that peer either and there is no gap there.
evidence: Container /Users/sen/common-lisp/bl-ga11v-misc-s3d, warm image, probe-g.lisp, on a real loopback TCP pair (open-listener / make-tcp-connection / accept-connection). The client wrote 12 of the 24 header bytes and stopped; one receive-message pass gave (:FIRST-PASS :CMD NIL :PAYLOAD :INCOMPLETE :IN-PROGRESS T :EXPIRED-NOW NIL). Backdating connection-recv-last-progress: (:AT-299S NIL) (:AT-301S T) (:AT-1199S-CORE-STILL-KEEPS-IT T) -- so the boundary is exactly 300 s and the peer is already gone at every point inside Core's 20-minute window. The trickle control: three rounds of backdating to 290 s and then delivering ONE byte gave (:AFTER-TRICKLE :IN-PROGRESS T :EXPIRED NIL :SECONDS-SINCE-PROGRESS 0), which is the measurement that turns this from 'slow peers are dropped' into 'only totally silent ones are'. Finally the pump entry point itself: backdated to 301 s, drain-and-reap-peer gave (:STATE-AFTER-EXPIRED-DRAIN :DISCONNECTED). Ours: src/networking/connection.lisp:592, :655-657, :668-679, :806-807; src/networking/ibd.lisp:1866-1871. Core: refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:2040-2046, refs/bitcoin/src/net.h:58-59.
fix_shape: Raise +receive-stall-timeout-seconds+ to Core's TIMEOUT_INTERVAL, 1200, and keep everything else as it is. The reaper itself should stay: Core's equivalent coverage comes from a socket handler that consults last_recv on every pass, and our pump has no such rule, so removing the in-progress reaper would leave a peer that sends a header and goes silent parked for the life of the connection -- which is the bug the reaper was added for. Making the two windows equal is what removes the divergence, and the docstring's justification for 300 already concedes the point: it argues the tight bound was needed only while the reader blocked, which it no longer does, so a stalled peer now costs one connection slot and at most +max-message-payload+ of buffer. If a rule for the not-yet-started case is wanted too, add Core's actual one -- disconnect on connection-last-recv-time older than 1200 seconds, which is already maintained (connection.lisp:818) and today read only by getpeerinfo -- rather than tightening the in-progress window. Any test must keep a trickle case as its positive control, since the whole severity of this finding turns on progress rather than elapsed time being the clock.
